name: Wason verbal illusion
aliases: No head injury is too trivial to be ignored
statement: Most readers take 'No head injury is too trivial to be ignored' to mean that every head injury should be treated, which is the reverse of what the words compose to.
meaning: The sentence has the shape No X is too Y to Z, and Wason and Reich argued that its compositional reading is an instruction to ignore all head injuries. Almost nobody reads it that way. Readers arrive instead at the sensible injunction. Wason and Reich reported that people shown the corrected sentence, No head injury is too trivial to be noticed, often called it ill-formed, and that attempts to put them right stirred feeling. Later authors call these depth charge sentences, a label Zhang and colleagues trace to Sanford and Emmott, because the implausibility goes unnoticed until someone points it out. Wason and Reich named three sources of trouble. The syntax carries up to four negations, a count they credit to Clark as a personal communication: the quantifier no, the implicit negation in too Y to Z, the negative adjective trivial, and the negative verb ignore. The construction too x to be y-ed normally means the more x, the less y, so too trivial to be ignored evokes a scale that runs backwards. And the compositional injunction contradicts what readers believe about head injuries. The name Wason verbal illusion comes from the title of their paper. The three studies since 2010 cited here all use the depth charge label instead.

origin.who: Peter C. Wason and Shuli S. Reich
origin.note: Their paper "A verbal illusion", volume 31, issue 4, pages 591 to 597, sets out the analysis and reports one experiment. The head injury sentence was not one of the items in that experiment.

evidence: Wason and Reich's abstract describes the whole of their experimental design: four pragmatic and four non-pragmatic sentences were paraphrased, and the prediction was confirmed that the pragmatic sentences were paraphrased more accurately. A sentence counts as pragmatic when its compositional injunction agrees with ordinary belief. No missile is too small to be banned amounts to ban all missiles, which is unremarkable. No error is too gross to be overlooked amounts to overlook all errors, which is not. The numbers behind that comparison are quoted here from Mark Liberman's 2009 Language Log summary of the paper rather than from the paper itself. Liberman reproduces the eight items, the instruction given to subjects, and the results table: 64 subjects, arranged as 16 pairs by two orders by two replications, each paraphrasing one sentence of each type. The four pragmatic sentences were paraphrased correctly on 51 of 64 occasions, or 80%. The four non-pragmatic sentences were paraphrased correctly on 27 of 64, or 42%. Item variation was wide, from 16 correct out of 16 for the missile sentence down to 3 out of 16 for No error is too gross to be overlooked. Wason and Reich also ran a pilot with content words removed. Shown No WUG is too DAX to be ZONGED, six of ten subjects took it to imply that WUGS should be ZONGED, which Wason and Reich treat as correct, and four of ten concluded the opposite. Paape, Vasishth and von der Malsburg report the same four out of ten. The head injury sentence itself was tested on nobody. Wason and Reich collected its misconstrual from letters sent by psychologists and linguists and from conversations, showing people the target on one side of a card and No head injury is too trivial to be noticed on the other. The paper itself could not be read on 21 September 2026. Taylor and Francis and SAGE both answer its PDF with a bot challenge rather than a paywall, and Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all record it closed. The Internet Archive holds the 1979 volume's contents, which confirm the title and pagination, but not the issue. Crossref carries the publisher's own abstract, and that is what is quoted above.

replication.headline: The inversion reappears in German, English, Danish and Greek, and German readers judged the depth charge condition the second most sensible of four conditions when it is the least sensible of them.
replication.detail: Paape, Vasishth and von der Malsburg ran five experiments in German, the first to measure the effect on-line rather than by paraphrase. Their Experiment 1 used 20 native speakers and 32 items crossing global negation with adjectival negation, rated for sensibleness on a seven-point scale. They fitted an ordinal cumulative logit model rather than a metric one, so its estimates sit on a latent scale and are not scale points. Adjectival negation cut ratings when global negation was absent, by an estimated 3.95, credible interval [-5.2, -2.72], and raised them when global negation was present, by 1.76, credible interval [0.88, 2.62]. The depth charge condition thus scored second only to the condition with no negation at all, though its compositional reading combines both anomalies. Whole-sentence reading times did not rise with each added negation, which is what a fully compositional reader should show. Experiment 2A added eye tracking with 61 participants and an operation span test, and found no sign that high working memory capacity protects against the inversion. Experiment 2B asked 35 people how far each item's intended meaning agreed with world knowledge, and those ratings were then used to re-analyse Experiment 2A's data. Items rated higher drew higher sensibleness ratings in the depth charge condition, a prediction Paape and colleagues call only partly borne out. Experiment 3 gave 60 readers three constructions, and found the inversion at equal strength in too ... to and too ... as that. The so ... that construction showed a smaller effect, which the authors are careful to call non-zero rather than absent. Experiment 4 found the illusion in sentence completions that stop before the final verb. Zhang, Ryskin and Gibson translated Paape's Experiment 1 items into English and ran them on Mechanical Turk, analysing 58 of 64 participants. The depth charge sentences drew a mean plausibility rating of 4.54, interval [4.37, 4.71], against 3.17 and 4.09 for the two other implausible conditions and 5.70 for the plausible control. Those figures are read from the submitted manuscript in MIT's repository, which is stamped as not peer reviewed. The version published in Cognition sits behind a ScienceDirect bot challenge, tried on 21 September 2026. Two earlier studies are known here only through Paape and colleagues' description of them. Natsopoulos used eight items in Greek and found that none of his 64 subjects derived the compositional meaning. A second study of his, offering three paraphrases to choose from, drew the compositional one about half the time. Kizach, Christensen and Weed gave 29 Danish speakers 150 sentences and found accuracy of about 40% in the depth charge condition, the lowest of their four conditions, with self-reported guessing at about 20%.

study.cite: Paape, D., Vasishth, S., & von der Malsburg, T. (2020). Quadruplex Negatio Invertit? The On-Line Processing of Depth Charge Sentences. Journal of Semantics, 37(4), 509-555.

limits: What replicates is the inversion, not Wason and Reich's explanation of it. Their guess that the final verb is where compositional processing breaks down survives their own paper poorly: Paape and colleagues found the inversion in sentence completions that never reach the verb. Their guess that four negations overload the reader predicts that readers with more working memory should resist, and Paape's eye-tracking experiment found no such relationship. Their guess that world knowledge drives the effect does better, and it is the one point where the evidence pulls in two directions. Paape's world knowledge norms and Zhang's rating study both find that world knowledge matters, though Paape calls the prediction only partly borne out. Natsopoulos, on Paape's account, found no link in his first study between how strongly his subjects held beliefs and how well they paraphrased, and some evidence for one in his third. The rival account is that No X is too Y to Z is a stored construction with two licensed meanings, so no processing failure occurs at all. Fortuin argues this from corpus examples, and Cook and Stevenson's model, described by Paape, classifies a construction's intended meaning from the lexical verb alone with 88% accuracy. Paape and colleagues conclude that their data fit specific variants of both accounts. The effect is also not confined to the classic four-negation frame. Paape quotes the attested No challenge is too big to stop us from saving our children from polio, which has no negative adjective.
misreadings: The sentence in the paper is "No head injury is too trivial to be ignored". The version that circulates drops the passive and reads "too trivial to ignore", and the two are not the same string even if they behave alike. Nobody in Wason and Reich's experiment saw either. Their eight test items were about missiles, governments, dictatorships, weather forecasts, errors, messages, films and books, and the famous 80% and 42% belong to those. The claim that the head injury sentence is almost invariably misconstrued rests in their paper on correspondence and conversation. Its provenance is thinner still. Gabriel Dupre, in a 2016 Language Log guest post, says only that it was allegedly found on the wall of a hospital triage department. Dupre also disputes the reading everyone treats as literal. From No head injury is too trivial to ignore it follows that triviality never blocks ignoring a head injury, and not that every head injury may be ignored, because some other predicate on the same scale may still block it. There is no contradiction in saying no head injury is too trivial to ignore but some are too serious to ignore. The illusion is not the Wason selection task, the four-card problem set out in entry no. 5, which shares nothing with it but the name Wason. It is distinct too from the Moses illusion, where readers answer 'two' to how many animals of each kind Moses took on the ark. That literature is larger and its numbers are lower. Umanath, Dolan and Marsh drew on a pool of 60 Moses illusion questions and gave 97 Duke undergraduates and 65 adults over 65 forty of them, half distorted. The younger group answered 41% of the distorted questions instead of flagging them, the older group 50%, t(160) = 2.51, Cohen's d = 0.40, p < .01. Both groups typed 'wrong' to 38% of the distorted questions, so the rate at which a reader catches the substitution is nearer two in five than one in two. A Czech replication of the font-readability manipulation gave 87 undergraduates two questions each, one of them distorted, and 43% of those in the hard-to-read condition reported the error against 37% in the easy one, with no effect of the font. Those are shares of people, not of trials. On the depth charge sentence, in Greek, none of 64 subjects derived the compositional meaning unaided.
